design_detail: Literature review (Addiction 2002;97:773-783; eleven pages, about 80 references) by three toxicologists at the Toxicology Laboratory, Leiden University Medical Center. It describes a search of Medline (from 1963), the Science Citation Index/Web of Science (from 1988) and Toxline (from 1980) in May to June 1999, repeated in October 2001, with English-language, human-only inclusion rules, but gives no count of records found, screened or excluded, no appraisal tool and no method of synthesis, so it is treated here as a narrative review. Results are split into prospective (laboratory) studies, summarised in Table 1 (14 studies), and retrospective studies (surveys, hospital, death and treatment samples); Tables 2 to 4 condense them. Read in full from the PDF, including the reference list; Tables 1 to 4 were checked on rendered pages 775 and 776. None of the cited studies was read for this card except McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998), which this library has read and which is used below to check how the review describes it.
can_establish: How three toxicologists, searching to 2001, summarised what small placebo-controlled laboratory studies and mostly uncontrolled retrospective studies had found about alcohol and cocaine taken together: blood levels, cocaethylene, heart rate, ratings of high and drunkenness, performance, and links to violence and other outcomes; and where they thought the evidence was thin.
cannot_establish: How large or how certain any effect is (no pooled estimate, no intervals, no counts of studies found or excluded); whether the combination adds more than the sum of its parts (the review itself says most studies do not test this); anything about smoked cocaine or about repeated high doses, which the laboratory studies did not use; whether cocaethylene or the higher cocaine level explains any heart-rate rise; whether the combination causes heart attacks or deaths (no controlled study of these is described); or what the primary studies found beyond what the review says about them.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (literature review). The 14 prospective studies in Table 1 had from 6 to 34 people each (13 had 12 or fewer; 147 participations in all by the editors' sum, with possible overlap between studies); the review does not describe who the volunteers were. Retrospective studies range from a national household survey of more than 25,000 people (1997) to a single case report; their number is not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Retrospective studies were included if they identified people who had used both alcohol and cocaine. Prospective studies were included if they used placebos, blind evaluation, a crossover design and appropriate presentation of data and statistics (Table 1); two between-subjects studies were kept despite design flaws. Excluded: studies comparing only alcohol with cocaine, studies not in humans, studies of 'polydrug' use and studies not in English (p. 774).
sample.selection_effects: Prospective studies all gave cocaine intranasally or by injection and never smoked (p. 774), mostly as single doses of 48 to 100 mg or 1.25 to 2 mg/kg, to volunteers whose drug history the review does not describe; the review itself says repeated high doses were not studied for ethical reasons, so toxicity of heavy binge use may be underestimated (p. 781). Retrospective studies sample people in emergency rooms, treatment programmes, crime and death records, who differ from people who combine the drugs and are never seen in these settings.

exposure.measurement: As described in the cited studies; not independently reported by the review. Blood levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol were measured in the laboratory studies; the retrospective studies rely on self-report, urine and blood tests in emergency rooms, and post-mortem findings.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, from Table 1: alcohol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (or 19.4 to 58.1 g) in most studies; cocaine intranasal, 48 to 100 mg or 1.25 to 2 mg/kg in most, 0.6 mg/kg intravenous in one and a radioactive tracer dose in one; one study gave four intranasal doses of 1 mg/kg (McCance-Katz and colleagues, 1998). In most studies the placebo was itself a 4 mg or 5 mg dose of cocaine (Table 1, footnote a).
exposure.polysubstance: 'Polydrug' studies were excluded from the review, yet several retrospective studies include people who also used other drugs (for example, the review's case report of a death involved cocaine, alcohol and cannabis); other-drug use is not controlled in the summaries.

comparison.controls: Prospective: placebo-controlled within-person crossover in 12 of 14 studies; two between-subjects studies (Pirwitz and colleagues, 1995, with 34 people having heart catheterisation for a medical reason; Volkow and Fowler, 1994, 7 people, no placebo and no blinding). Retrospective: many studies compare people who used both drugs with people who used cocaine alone and have no alcohol-only comparison group, which the review points out several times (pp. 778-779).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: In retrospective studies the people who combine the drugs differ in how much alcohol and cocaine they take, how they take cocaine (for example, smoked or not) and other features; the review notes this for some studies (Castaneda and colleagues, 1995; Easton and Bauer, 1997) but offers no adjusted analysis.

outcomes.instruments: Outcomes are those of the cited studies: heart rate, blood pressure, rate-pressure product, coronary artery diameter, rating scales for high and drunkenness, performance tests, EEG, blood levels, hospital and death records, interviews.
outcomes.operationalization: Effects are judged as additive, 'greater-than-additive' (called potentiation by the review), subtractive or inhibitive, after Berenbaum (1977, 1989); the review says only a few studies met Berenbaum's criterion of at least two active doses of each drug, and uses 'potentiation' loosely for that reason (p. 774).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled analysis. Figures the review gives from other studies: blood cocaine up to 30% higher when cocaine was given with or after alcohol (five studies; Table 1 gives 30% for a 6-person study and 15% for McCance-Katz and colleagues, 1998); blood alcohol unchanged or about 10% lower (non-significant) when cocaine followed alcohol; 57 of 451 cocaine-positive hospital urine samples (12.6%) contained cocaethylene (Bailey, 1995); 88% of people positive for both alcohol and cocaine in more than 1,000 emergency-room screens had cocaethylene (Signs and colleagues, 1996); 21 of 600 and 12 of 285 fatally injured drivers positive for both drugs (Los Angeles County; Spain); 40% against 26% severely beating someone and 39% against 24% threatening with a weapon among 320 male veterans in cocaine treatment who used the combination against cocaine alone (Denison and colleagues, 1997); three times and five times as likely to have homicidal ideas or plans as people who used alcohol only or cocaine only (Salloum and colleagues, 1996).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; search dates are given (May to June 1999, repeated October 2001).
analysis.selective_reporting: No counts of records identified, screened or excluded; no list of the retrospective studies considered; no appraisal of the prospective studies beyond the inclusion filter; the two included studies with a between-subjects design, one of which had no placebo and no blinding, do not meet the review's own stated inclusion rules.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the review does not comment that most laboratory studies had 12 or fewer people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Fourteen small laboratory studies, with caveats the review lists, found that alcohol taken with or before cocaine was followed by higher blood cocaine (up to 30%) and by cocaethylene, that heart-rate rises were at least additive, with a trend towards greater than additive in most studies (the review says only a few had the two active doses of each drug needed to test this), that ratings of cocaine high tended to rise and ratings of drunkenness tended to fall a little (Table 1 labels two of the three reported falls non-significant), and that cocaine lessened some alcohol-impaired test performance; one 6-person study that gave alcohol after cocaine did not find the heart-rate or blood-cocaine excess. Retrospective studies show frequent co-use, no clear cardiovascular excess in emergency-room data but without alcohol-only comparison groups, and mostly alcohol-attributable violence with one study of homicidal ideas pointing to more than alcohol or cocaine alone.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says there is generally no evidence that the combination does more than add up the effects of each drug, with exceptions: cocaine works against alcohol's deficits; heart-rate effects 'tend' to be greater than additive; cocaethylene 'may potentiate' cardiotoxic effects; and, 'more importantly', retrospective data suggest the combination can potentiate violent thoughts and threats. Table 3 gives a 'greater-than-additive increase' in high, and Table 4 gives a 'more-than-additive risk' of birth defects. The conclusions say the combination does not cause more cardiovascular problems than expected from additive effects.

timeline.event: Foltin and Fischman (Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior; as described by this review, not read): greater-than-additive heart-rate effects with smaller doses and additive effects with higher doses of alcohol and cocaine
Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat (Life Sciences; as described by this review, not read): alcohol before cocaine; additive heart-rate rise, higher blood cocaine and cocaethylene
Farre and colleagues and McCance-Katz and colleagues (as described by this review, not read): cocaethylene formed and blood cocaine higher with alcohol
Perez-Reyes (Life Sciences; as described by this review, not read): 6 people; alcohol 30 minutes after cocaine; no excess in blood cocaine or heart rate; cocaethylene still formed
McCance-Katz, Kosten and Jatlow: four doses of intranasal cocaine in 8 people; heart rate and blood cocaine higher with alcohol, cocaethylene formed
This review; no later laboratory studies are included

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source. The laboratory findings it summarises (higher blood cocaine, cocaethylene, a heart-rate rise at least as large as the sum, a modest fall in drunkenness ratings) come from about a dozen studies of 6 to 12 people each, several of which share first authors (Farre, Foltin, Higgins, McCance-Katz, Perez-Reyes) and so may not be independent; the review does not discuss this. The only primary study of the 14 that this library has read (McCance-Katz and colleagues, 1998) agrees in direction, but the review describes it in ways the primary paper does not support (see reporting issues).

funding.funder: The Nationaal Instituut voor Gezondheidsbevordering en Ziektepreventie (NIGZ), the Brijderstichting and the Jellinek (Acknowledgements, p. 781); the paper does not say what these bodies are or what they funded beyond 'this study'.
funding.affiliations_note: Toxicology Laboratory, Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, the Netherlands. None of the three authors appears in the reference list.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a registered protocol, counts at each step, a risk-of-bias judgment for each primary study and effect sizes with intervals; new placebo-controlled studies with at least two doses of each drug, both orders of dosing, smoked cocaine, heart rhythm and blood-pressure outcomes and a test of additivity; and cohort or case-crossover studies of heart events and injury that include alcohol-only and cocaine-only comparison groups.

domains.note: Databases, years, search terms, language and design rules are stated, and the search was repeated before revision; but no counts of records found or excluded, no screening method and no list of retrospective studies are given.

Prospective studies were filtered on placebo, blinding, crossover and data presentation; the review repeatedly points out missing alcohol-only comparison groups, between-subjects designs and untested tracer doses; but it does not comment on sample sizes of 6 to 12 people, one-tailed testing, or the 4 to 5 mg cocaine placebo.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the three authors appears in the reference list.

Mechanisms are hedged in the text ('may be due to', 'one possible explanation'), and the text says the cocaethylene discussion 'may be premature'; but the abstract says cocaethylene 'may potentiate' cardiotoxic effects, Table 3 states a greater-than-additive rise in high, and Table 4 states a more-than-additive risk of birth defects from one case report.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the main conclusions
domains.note: The text reports contrary findings (no cardiovascular excess in emergency-room data; people using both drugs doing better on some tests; one laboratory study with no excess when alcohol followed cocaine), but the abstract gives violence the weight of 'more importantly' although the two violent-behaviour studies lack alcohol-only comparison groups and the one controlled study, which concerns thoughts, needs replication, as the review says.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is more transparent than most narrative reviews about how studies were found, and it points out many weaknesses in its sources; but it cannot show that its set of studies is complete, it summarises effect sizes only as a 'trend towards greater-than-additive' and as 'up to' figures, and it describes at least one primary study in ways that study does not support. It may be cited for what a 2002 review reported about blood cocaine, cocaethylene, heart rate and ratings of drunkenness in small laboratory studies, for the rates of co-use it quotes, and for its own list of what the retrospective evidence lacks. It may not be cited for the size of any effect, for an order-of-dosing rule, for toxicity of the combination, for violence, or for birth defects.

key_findings.finding: The abstract concludes there is generally no evidence that alcohol and cocaine together do more than add up the effects of each drug, with exceptions: cocaine consistently works against alcohol-induced deficits in learning, psychomotor performance and driving; heart-rate effects tend to be greater than additive, with up to 30% higher blood cocaine; cocaethylene may potentiate cardiotoxic effects; and retrospective data suggest the combination can potentiate violent thoughts and threats.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: Search: Medline (from 1963), Science Citation Index/Web of Science (from 1988) and Toxline (from 1980); done May to June 1999 and repeated October 2001. Excluded: studies comparing only alcohol with cocaine, studies not in humans, studies of 'polydrug' use and studies not in English. No count of records identified, screened or excluded is given.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (continues onto p. 774) and 2nd paragraph (p. 774); Inclusion and exclusion, 1st paragraph (p. 774)

key_findings.finding: Prospective studies were included if they used placebos, blind evaluation, a crossover design and appropriate data presentation; two between-subjects studies were kept despite design flaws (Pirwitz and colleagues, 1995, with heart catheterisation for a medical reason; Volkow and Fowler, 1994, with radiolabelled tracer). Prospective studies gave cocaine only intranasally or intravenously, never smoked. Only a few studies had at least two active doses of each drug, so the review uses 'potentiation' in place of 'synergism'.
key_findings.locator: Inclusion and exclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists 14 prospective studies with 6 to 34 people each (13 had 12 or fewer). Alcohol 0.5 to 1 g/kg in most; cocaine intranasal, mostly 48 to 100 mg or 1.25 to 2 mg/kg; in most studies the placebo was a 4 mg or 5 mg dose of cocaine. Pirwitz and colleagues are listed as 'within' although the text calls that study between-subjects.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and footnote a

key_findings.finding: Alcohol-induced deficits in the laboratory were consistently lessened by cocaine: digit-symbol substitution (Foltin and colleagues, 1993; Higgins and colleagues, 1993), sedation (Foltin and colleagues, 1993), and learning and psychomotor performance (Higgins and colleagues, 1992).
key_findings.locator: Results > Prospective research > Behavioural

key_findings.finding: Heart rate: when cocaine was given at the same time as or after alcohol, most studies showed a trend towards greater-than-additive effects but did not support the idea that the effects are synergistic; studies with at least two active doses of each drug are needed. Table 1 gives greater-than-additive rises in four studies (Farre 1993, Farre 1997, Higgins 1993, McCance-Katz 1998), additive rises in two (McCance-Katz 1993; Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat, 1992), and greater-than-additive rises at smaller doses with additive rises at higher doses in one (Foltin and Fischman, 1988).
key_findings.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 1st paragraph (p. 774); Table 1 (p. 775)

key_findings.finding: One study of 34 people (Pirwitz and colleagues, 1995) found that the combination raised the rate-pressure product (a measure of the heart's oxygen demand) with a concomitant rise in the width of the coronary artery; the review says the limits of its between-subjects design apply.
key_findings.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Order of dosing: in a 6-person study with alcohol given 30 minutes after cocaine (35 in Table 1), heart-rate increases were additive in the text and 'no effect' in Table 1, blood cocaine was not higher than with cocaine alone, and 'high' did not change, whereas with alcohol first the earlier studies found greater-than-additive heart-rate rises; cocaethylene formed in both. The review calls alcohol before cocaine the more common order, without a source.
key_findings.locator: Heart rate, 2nd paragraph (pp. 774, 776); Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 776); Effect on perceived inebriation, 2nd paragraph (p. 777); Table 1 (p. 775)
key_findings.note: One small study; cited here as a limit on how far the heart-rate and blood-level results generalise, not as a finding about what people do.

key_findings.finding: Blood levels: cocaine given at the same time as or after alcohol raised blood cocaine by up to 30% (five studies). Blood alcohol was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, non-significantly, in four; the review offers competitive inhibition of cocaine-metabolising esterases and cocaine-related vasoconstriction slowing alcohol absorption as possible explanations, and says cocaethylene is too small to account for the lower alcohol levels.
key_findings.locator: Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Alcohol had no effect on the uptake or clearance of radiolabelled tracer cocaine from the brain or heart in 7 people; the review notes that study had no placebo, no blinding and a tracer dose that may not generalise to active doses.
key_findings.locator: Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Perceived drunkenness: several studies found cocaine produced a slight decrease (Farre 1993, Higgins 1993, Farre 1997), one found no effect (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat, 1992); Table 1 labels the Farre falls 'non-significantly reduced drunk'. Ratings of cocaine 'high' or global intoxication were greater when alcohol was given before or with cocaine in six studies; EEG indices of intoxication matched in one (Mannelli and colleagues, 1993); alcohol pretreatment raised preference for cocaine over cash in one study (Higgins and colleagues, 1996).
key_findings.locator: Effect on perceived inebriation, 1st paragraph (pp. 776–777); Table 1 (p. 775)

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene was made only when both drugs were given, never with either alone (six studies), and was also made when alcohol came 30 minutes after cocaine. The review says it has similar behavioural and toxicological effects to cocaine, slightly less potent, and that people could not tell it from cocaine when given intranasally or by injection.
key_findings.locator: Cocaethylene production

key_findings.finding: Co-use in surveys and clinical samples: a 1990 US survey estimated about 4 million people used alcohol and cocaine at the same time in the previous month and 9 million in the previous year; in the 1997 National Household Survey (over 25,000 people) people who drank in the past month were six times as likely, and those who drank heavily eight times as likely, to have used cocaine in the past month; 43% of 3,762 emergency-room patients in 1983–1993 had used cocaine, about a third of them with alcohol; 57% and 61% of people in cocaine treatment were also alcohol-dependent; about 60% of cocaine- or crack-using patients in a methadone programme reported using alcohol to come down.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Extent of use, 1st paragraph (p. 777) and 2nd paragraph (p. 778)

key_findings.finding: Driving: retrospective research points to a major role for alcohol alone; the combination gave no definitive protection, since 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain were positive for both.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Operating motor vehicles, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene in hospital samples: 57 of 451 cocaine-positive urine samples (12.6%) contained it, 53 from emergency or trauma patients, with higher mean blood alcohol in the positive samples (1.3 against 0.6 g/l); in 18 emergency patients positive for alcohol and cocaine, 11 had cocaethylene; in more than 1,000 emergency screens, 88% of those positive for both had it, and its level correlated with cocaine; a second laboratory found no correlation.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review says whether cocaethylene or a higher cocaine level explains the heart-rate rise is controversial and that the talk of greater cardiotoxicity may be premature: no retrospective study shows unequivocally that the combination causes more; one study of more than 1,000 emergency screens found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one; another found less chest pain but more back and limb pain with the combination, without an alcohol-only group.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 2nd paragraph (pp. 778–779)

key_findings.finding: A single case report of an 18-year-old who died suddenly of cardiotoxicity after cocaine, alcohol and cannabis (unknown dose and schedule) is set against the 1,000-patient study that found a predominant role for cocaine alone.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 3rd (last) paragraph

key_findings.finding: Violence: many studies found a predominant role for alcohol; two studies suggest more violent behaviour with the combination but have no alcohol-only comparison group (emergency-room trauma: 50% combination against 22% cocaine only; 320 male veterans in treatment: 40% against 26% severely beat someone); one 'well-designed' study found the combination three times as likely as alcohol only and five times as likely as cocaine only to go with homicidal ideas or plans, which the review says must be replicated.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Violence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Neuropsychology: mixed; four studies found people using the combination in some ways better off than those using one drug; the review suggests that opposing effects or differences in dose and route (for example, less smoked crack) may explain this.
key_findings.locator: Neuropsychology and psychiatry, paragraph beginning 'There are four studies' (p. 780)

key_findings.finding: Birth defects: a single case report of one child exposed to both drugs in pregnancy; Table 4 records this as 'more-than-additive risk (one report found)'.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 776); Liver function, HIV risk and teratology, last paragraph (p. 780)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: prospective studies show greater feeling of intoxication from the combination (high), no or opposing effect on alcohol drunkenness and lessened alcohol deficits; heart-rate increases 'statistically additive' with a trend towards greater than additive; retrospective studies suggest no more cardiovascular problems than additive expectations and show flawed emergency-room data lacking alcohol-only controls; high repeated cocaine doses have not been studied, so the behavioural toxicity of heavy binge use with alcohol may be underestimated.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes the participants of McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998) as showing the usual 'alcohol first' pattern of effects, with greater-than-additive increases in heart rate, plasma cocaine and 'high'; the primary paper gave the first cocaine dose first with alcohol immediately after (as the review's own Table 1 footnote b says), compared the combination only with each drug alone (never against the sum), and found 'any high' not significant (p = .09).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's table and text overstate this study; cite the primary paper for what it found. The same slip may affect other rows, which could not be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Table 3 say the combination gives a 'greater-than-additive' rise in high, but the text and Table 1 show additive effects (Mannelli 1993; McCance-Katz 1993), no or variable effects (Higgins 1993; Perez-Reyes 1994) and non-significant increases (Farre 1993, 1997).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the text, not Table 3, for how consistent the 'high' findings are.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says retrospective data suggest the combination potentiates violent thoughts and threats and calls this 'more importantly' a finding, but in the text the two violent-behaviour studies lack alcohol-only comparison groups and the one controlled study concerns homicidal ideas, not threats, and 'must be replicated'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weight the abstract gives to violence is not supported by the studies as the review describes them.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 states 'more-than-additive risk (one report found)' for birth defects, and the text shows that report is a single case of one child.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single case cannot show risk of any size; the table treats a case report as a risk statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says cocaethylene 'may potentiate' cardiotoxic effects, while the text says that part of the discussion may be premature, that no retrospective study shows greater cardiotoxicity, and that the best-sized study (over 1,000 emergency screens) found no excess with the combination.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text, not the abstract, represents the evidence on heart harm.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1990 US survey figures on simultaneous use of alcohol and cocaine are cited to a paper whose title (Grant and Harford, 1990) concerns alcohol with sedatives and tranquilizers; the source was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: The attribution cannot be checked here; use the survey figures only as quoted by the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's summary of blood alcohol (no effect or about a 10% non-significant fall) omits McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998), whose own paper reports significantly lower blood alcohol with cocaine (p = .008; 99 against 118 mg/dL, 30 minutes after the second drink).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review understates the fall in blood alcohol seen in the one multiple-dose study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says cocaine consistently works against alcohol-induced learning, psychomotor and driving deficits, but the text describes no prospective test of driving (the laboratory findings concern digit-symbol substitution, sedation, learning and psychomotor tasks), and the retrospective section and the conclusions say alcohol alone has the major role in driving deficits, with no evidence that cocaine adds to them and no definitive protection from them (21 of 600 and 12 of 285 fatally injured drivers positive for both).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the laboratory findings for test performance only; the review gives no basis for saying that cocaine lessens the effect of alcohol on driving.

reporting_issues.issue: Small details do not match between the table and the text: Pirwitz and colleagues are 'within' in Table 1 but between-subjects in the text; Perez-Reyes (1994) has 'no effect on heart rate' and alcohol 35 minutes after cocaine in Table 1 but additive heart-rate rises and 30 minutes in the text; two studies by Foltin give different middle alcohol doses (38.7 and 38.1 g) in Table 1; the Volkow and Fowler study fails the review's own inclusion rules (no placebo, no blinding) but is included.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary tables cannot be relied on for detail without the primary papers.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 773-783 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Pennings_2002_AlcoholCocaineConcurrent.pdf), full text including Tables 1 to 4 and the reference list; Tables 1 to 4 checked against rendered pages 775 and 776. The cited primary studies were not read except McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998).
